summary: Cast specimen (as-solidified ingot) of a high-Al added low-density medium Mn steel of designed grade Fe-8Mn-5Al-0.2C (wt.%). It is the base/solidified state produced by the conventional melting-casting route in an open-air induction furnace, on which the paper's later homogenization, hot forging, hot rolling and intercritical annealing sequence is built. The specimen serves as the starting point for studying phase transformation and austenite stability, and already exhibits a duplex delta ferrite + austenite microstructure with dendritic austenite.
composition: Nominal designed grade: Fe-8Mn-5Al-0.2C (wt.%), a low-density medium Mn steel (medium Mn: 3-12 wt.% Mn). Measured bulk chemistry (XRF and OES, Table 1, wt.%): Fe balance, Mn 7.79, Al 4.88, Si 0.84, C 0.2, P 0.03, S 0.03. Al (~5 wt.%) and Si (~1 wt.%) are added as lightening elements - Al lowers density while both Al and Si stabilise ferrite; Mn and C are the austenite stabilisers. The high Al level (and Si) is also the reason delta ferrite forms instead of a fully austenitic structure.
processing: The designed alloy was produced by the conventional melting-casting route in an open-air induction furnace (Power Trak 250-10 R Inductotherm), without a controlled atmosphere. The as-solidified cast ingot is the "cast specimen" state; no thermal or mechanical step is applied to it prior to characterization. In the overall process genealogy this cast ingot is the precursor from which all other states are derived: it is subsequently homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 h, hot forged to 50% thickness reduction in the 1050-800 °C range followed by air cooling, then hot rolled (soaking at 1100 °C for 2 h) in the 1050-800 °C range in two passes with 50% reduction per pass and water quenching, and finally intercritically annealed at 750 °C for 5, 30, 60, 120 and 180 min. The alloy design targets a theoretical stacking fault energy of ~35 mJ/m² (Olson-Cohen model, initial austenite grain size assumed 40 µm), placing it in the 20-40 mJ/m² TWIP range; Thermo-Calc (TCFE9) predicts a duplex delta ferrite + austenite region from ~650 °C to ~1350 °C with the equilibrium sequence L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → γ+δ, so BCC phase persists on cooling from the liquid (>~1500 °C) to room temperature.
microstructure: Dual-phase microstructure of delta ferrite (δ, BCC) and austenite (γ, FCC) in the cast ingot, confirmed by both XRD and optical microscopy. Rietveld refinement of XRD data gives ~70 volume% δ-ferrite (matrix) and ~26 volume% austenite. The austenite in the cast specimen has a dendritic type structure (marked by blue arrows in the optical micrographs, Fig. 2b,c), i.e. coarse plate/needle-like second-phase features in a lighter ferrite matrix. XRD reflections are indexed as α110, γ111, γ200, α200, γ220, α211, γ311 and γ222 (α: ferrite (δ/α), γ: austenite). Because the Thermo-Calc equilibrium plot shows BCC persisting from the liquid down to room temperature, the ferrite present is identified as δ-ferrite formed during solidification. The high (~5 wt.%) Al addition prevents complete austenitization and enhances δ-ferrite stability, so the ferrite is not consumed by austenite. The high δ-ferrite fraction (~70 vol%) is expected to accelerate C and Mn diffusion into austenite and thereby raise austenite stability. Comparison with the hot forged specimen (~29 vol% austenite, only ~3% higher) indicates little variation in austenite fraction between cast and forged states, though some elemental partitioning during soaking may occur.
properties: Physical: density of the developed steel measured by Archimedes' principle is 6.91455 g/cc, i.e. ~11.35% lower than conventional steel (~7.8 g/cc), achieved by the ~5 wt.% Al and ~1 wt.% Si additions. No tensile, hardness or other mechanical properties are reported for the cast specimen itself. Characterization performed on the cast specimen: X-ray diffraction (Bruker D8 advanced diffractometer, Co-Kα 1.79 Å target, step size 0.02°, 2θ 20°-120°) for phase identification; Rietveld refinement of the XRD data for phase volume fractions; and optical microscopy (Leica) after standard metallography with colloidal polishing (0.25 µm) and etching in Villella's Reagent (5 ml HCl + 1 g picric acid + 100 ml ethanol) for 10-15 s. Results were corroborated by an overall characterization suite used across the study (SEM/EDS on ZEISS VP 300, EBSD, dilatometry, HRTEM, APT, nanoindentation and tensile testing), though these were applied to the forged, rolled/quenched and annealed states rather than to the cast specimen.
mechanisms: Solidification pathway control by high Al: Thermo-Calc (TCFE9) predicts the sequence L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → γ+δ with BCC phase persisting from the liquid (>~1500 °C) to room temperature; because ~5 wt.% Al suppresses complete austenitization and stabilises δ-ferrite, the BCC ferrite in the cast specimen forms directly during solidification and survives cooling instead of being consumed by austenite.

Dendritic austenite morphology: the austenite in the cast ingot solidifies with a dendritic/plate-like morphology (visible in optical micrographs), a solidification signature that is only partially erased by later soaking before hot forging - remnant dendrites are still visible in the forged specimen due to insufficient soaking/dissolution.

δ-ferrite as a diffusion accelerator for austenite stabilisation: the high ~70 vol% δ-ferrite fraction is expected to accelerate C and Mn diffusion into austenite during isothermal holding, enriching austenite in austenite-stabilising elements and increasing its stability - which is why the cast/forged austenite resists decomposition into low-temperature transformation products on cooling to room temperature.

Duplex stability and negligible transformation contraction: because the austenite does not decompose into α-ferrite, pearlite or martensite at room temperature and only a small fraction of δ-ferrite dissolves on heating, the dilatometry curve of the forged state (the cast descendant) shows no significant contraction - only a slight deviation at ~600 °C attributable to possible carbide/cementite and minor ferrite dissolution.

Stacking fault energy as a design lever: adding Al strongly raises the SFE of austenite (theoretical ~35 mJ/m² with equilibrium austenite composition), placing the alloy in the 20-40 mJ/m² TWIP window; however, elemental partitioning and morphology changes produced by thermomechanical treatment and intercritical annealing can lower the reverted austenite SFE (e.g. to ~27 mJ/m² at 60 min), which shifts the deformation mechanism toward TRIP.
conclusions: The cast specimen is the as-solidified baseline of the developed Fe-8Mn-5Al-0.2C (measured Fe-7.79Mn-4.88Al-0.84Si-0.2C, wt.%) low-density medium Mn steel, produced by conventional open-air melting-casting. It establishes two facts that frame the rest of the study: (i) the duplex δ-ferrite + austenite structure with dendritic austenite forms already during solidification and is inherited from the high-Al chemistry rather than created by thermomechanical processing; and (ii) the alloy attains a density of 6.91455 g/cc, ~11.35% below conventional steel, confirming high Al (~5 wt.%) plus Si (~1 wt.%) as an effective lightening strategy. Relative to the hot forged state (~29 vol% austenite) the cast state retains a similar austenite fraction (~26 vol%, only ~3% lower), showing that forging/homogenisation does not strongly alter the phase balance; subsequent hot rolling plus water quenching introduces lenticular martensite, and intercritical annealing at 750 °C then drives reverted austenite formation, with 60 min giving the optimum austenite stability, the highest transformation ratio and the best strength-ductility combination (UTS 658.45±6 MPa, total elongation 12±0.95%). The cast specimen therefore serves as the reference condition from which the phase-transformation and austenite-stability narrative of the paper develops.
unmapped: The designed grade is described as a low-density medium Mn steel of nominal composition Fe-8Mn-5Al-0.2C (wt.%), consistent with the measured values in Table 1.

Elemental analysis in this study was performed with at least 5-7 areas and 15-20 spots per phase, reporting averages with standard deviation (SEM ZEISS VP 300 with EDAX) - methodology applied to the developed steel, the derivative states rather than specifically to the cast specimen.

Thermo-Calc phase-fraction plot (Fig. 1b) additionally lists minor phases kappa_E21, cementite, M23C6, CUB_A13, FE8SI2C and CBCC_A12, but all remain near zero fraction and are not resolved in the cast specimen's microstructure.

No carbide (e.g. kappa-carbide) precipitation was detected in the steel; in the IA750_60 Min state HRTEM/APT found no precipitates or elemental clustering, only Mn/C enrichment and Al depletion at the reverted austenite / intercritical ferrite interface.
